title: Indian IT Stocks Jumped 18% in October. Earnings Will Decide What Next
excerpt: The Nifty IT index posted its best month in over six years as the global AI trade cooled. September-quarter results beat low expectations and AI revenue is now material — but analysts say December-quarter conversion is the real test.
body:
• Indian IT was October's strongest sector: the Nifty IT index rose 17.69% in the month, its best monthly performance in more than six years, while the Nifty 50 gained 1.91%.
  • September-quarter results were better than feared but uneven: BNP Paribas counted 60% of IT firms beating revenue estimates and 53% beating margin expectations, while Wipro guided its December quarter to between -1.5% and +0.5%.
  • AI is already material revenue: TCS reported an annualised AI revenue run rate of $3.1 billion — over a tenth of quarterly revenue — and Infosys said AI revenue grew 29% from the previous quarter.
  • The test is conversion, not sentiment: Greyhound Research says December-quarter bookings must turn into sequential growth above 2% across the four largest firms for the rally to rest on substance.

Indian information technology stocks have had their best month in more than six years. The Nifty IT index advanced 17.69% in October to close at 32,606.90 on October 30, far outperforming the Nifty 50's 1.91% gain, according to Motilal Oswal data reported by The Hindu BusinessLine. The rebound followed months of selling driven by cautious client budgets and fears that AI would disrupt the sector's labour-based model. The question analysts are now asking is narrower: do the earnings support the prices?

What the September quarter actually showed

The results were better than the low expectations set for them. BNP Paribas noted that IT services companies reported slightly ahead of estimates for the September quarter, with 60% of firms beating revenue estimates and 53% beating EBIT margin expectations, BusinessLine reported. The detail, compiled by 5paisa, shows a selective rather than uniform recovery: TCS grew constant-currency revenue 0.5% sequentially with a 24.0% operating margin and $9.6 billion in total contract value; Infosys grew 1.2% with a 21.0% margin and $5.2 billion in large-deal wins, but guided FY27 revenue growth to just 1-2% in constant-currency terms; HCLTech grew 2.3% with $3.26 billion in new deals. Wipro was the laggard, reporting flat sequential constant-currency IT services revenue and guiding the December quarter to between -1.5% and +0.5%.

Two different rallies are being confused

Part of October's rise was rotation: as the global AI trade weakened, Indian IT's lower valuations and distance from AI infrastructure spending attracted buyers. Nomura said it expects relative sentiment toward Indian equities among foreign investors to improve, supported by low starting expectations and the correction in AI stocks, with the Nifty outperforming the AI-heavy indices of Korea, Taiwan and the Nasdaq. Yugal Joshi, a partner at Everest Group, was blunter: "It's a sentiment-driven market and valuations have become attractive," he told BusinessLine.

"A rally built on AI stocks falling treats Indian IT as a business that AI hurts. The firms' own growth case runs the other way, with AI now above a tenth of revenue at TCS and Infosys."

— Sanchit Vir Gogia, Chief Analyst and Founder, Greyhound Research

Gogia set the test for what comes next: if December-quarter bookings convert into sequential growth above 2% across the four largest firms, "the substance will have caught up with the timing." The AI revenue figures give that test something to measure. TCS said its annualised AI revenue run rate reached $3.1 billion, crossing 10% of quarterly revenue; HCLTech reported advanced AI revenue of $219 million, up 28.4% sequentially in constant-currency terms; Infosys said AI revenue grew 29% from the previous quarter, according to 5paisa's compilation of company disclosures.

The spending backdrop is narrower than the headline

Global technology budgets are growing, but not evenly. Gartner's October forecast, cited by 5paisa, puts worldwide IT spending at about $7.35 trillion in 2027, up 15% from 2026 — yet spending on IT services specifically is expected to grow a more modest 4.9% in 2027, with the expansion concentrated in data-centre infrastructure, AI platforms and software. That split is the sector's real contest: budgets are moving toward cloud, modernisation, cybersecurity and AI work, and firms that win it can outperform those dependent on legacy service lines, while AI tools that let clients do development and support work with fewer billed hours press on traditional pricing.

This rotation argument is also the one a senior Indian government official made this week about the Nvidia-led reset in AI valuations — we covered that claim, and its counter-evidence, here: AI Valuation Reset Could Benefit Indian IT Firms, Senior Official Says. The earnings data point the same way but prove less: October's advance does not by itself confirm durable momentum, and the index remains below its 52-week high. For diaspora investors holding Indian IT through mutual funds or direct listings, the December-quarter results — deal conversion and constant-currency growth, not index levels — are the evidence that will settle whether this was a recovery or a reprieve.
